category: O-F2 Laser, lens and camera-side optical attacks
title: Adversarial Lens Flares: A Threat to Camera-Based Systems in Smart Devices
venue: IEEE Internet of Things Journal
key_idea: Lens flare from an ordinary flashlight, placed so it overlaps the target, works as a physical adversarial perturbation against sign and object recognition by day and night; a closed-box digital flare attack supports large-scale tests.
method: Physical flashlight flare tests in traffic scenes plus a black-box digital attack that pastes real flare images as perturbations.
data: GTSRB; MTSD (Mapillary Traffic Sign Dataset); physical traffic scenes
reported_result: Abstract: physical flashlight flare reaches an average attack success rate above 90 percent day and night; digital attack success up to 95.4 percent on GTSRB and 82.8 percent on MTSD against YOLOv8, DINOv2 and three other models.
relation_to_project: Threatens P-c and P-d directly: lens flare is the benign look-alike a light guard is meant to tolerate, so a rule that excuses every flare-shaped artefact can be exploited (N3, N4). Strong test case for a flare-versus-attack decision.
notes: Abstract read from the DOI record shown in a search result (Crossref record has no abstract). Published online 2024-12-18, issue year 2025 (vol 12 no 9). Abstract discusses defenses only briefly.

category: O-F3 Exposure, HDR and pulsed-light effects
title: AdvLIM-LD: Toward Cross-Task Physical Adversarial Attack via LED Illumination Modulation for Lane Detection Systems
venue: IEEE Internet of Things Journal
key_idea: Pulse-width-modulated LED light plus the CMOS rolling shutter writes invisible brightness stripes into captured frames; a critical-feature loss makes the perturbation transfer across lane-detection model types.
method: Critical feature detection module, joint optimisation of feature loss and output accuracy loss, LED PWM modulation exploiting rolling-shutter readout.
data: Lane detection models SCNN, LaneATT, LSTR, GANet; physical-world tests
reported_result: Abstract: average detection accuracy drop of 74.64 percent across four lane models in simulation, 55.37 percent in cross-task attacks, and over 80 percent on source models in physical tests.
relation_to_project: Direct evidence for P-d and N4: flicker invisible to people but visible to the sensor as row-wise banding; a guard that looks for row-periodic luminance residuals is the matching check. Lane task, not object detection.
notes: Abstract read from the DOI record shown in a search result. Journal extension of a PRCV 2023 conference paper (doi 10.1007/978-981-99-8435-0_38, not verified in this run). Same group as MLIA (P2-P425).

category: O-F5 Defenses against light-patch attacks
title: Laser Shield: a Physical Defense with Polarizer against Laser Attacks on Autonomous Driving Systems
venue: Proceedings of the 61st ACM/IEEE Design Automation Conference (DAC 2024)
key_idea: Lasers are polarised while daylight and LED light are not, so a rotating polariser in front of the camera, steered by a cheap RGB-energy minimum, suppresses adversarial laser beams before inference.
method: Hardware polariser on a rotator with min-energy angle search; compared with bit-depth reduction, pixel deflection and a diffusion clean-up model.
data: LAPA physical laser dataset (300 images, 27 scenes); digital simulation; three on-road scenes
reported_result: Paper text (authors' copy, seen in a search result, not the abstract): on LAPA defense success rate 100 percent and functionality-preserving rate 100 percent; fault tolerance rate 60.0 percent; baselines 33.3 to 88.9 percent success.
relation_to_project: Baseline and counterpoint for designs 3 and 4: a hardware optical filter, not a software guard; it covers polarised laser light only, not projectors, LEDs or flares. Its benign-preservation metric is a model for the guard's false-alarm reporting.
code_or_data: LAPA dataset named in the abstract; location not seen UNVERIFIED
notes: Abstract read on the ACM page shown in a search result; numbers come from the paper body shown in the same search result. Evaluated on a ResNet50 classifier, not a detector; not deployed on a vehicle (paper says so).

category: O-F1 Projector and projected-light attacks
title: Spoofing Mobileye 630’s Video Camera Using a Projector
venue: Proceedings Third International Workshop on Automotive and Autonomous Vehicle Security (AutoSec 2021)
key_idea: A projected road sign, even with wrong colours, makes a commercial ADAS (Mobileye 630 PRO) issue false sign notifications; shape matters, colour does not; a drone-borne projector delivers it while driving.
method: Real car with Mobileye 630 PRO; varied projected size, colour, shape, duration, ambient light; drone-mounted projector demo.
data: Physical drives (Renault Captur with Mobileye 630 PRO)
reported_result: Paper text: a 100 ms projection was enough; signs under 16 cm diameter were not detected; detection distance about 5 to 16 m; injection worked at all hours, best in the evening and at night.
relation_to_project: Real-system evidence for P-d and N3: a phantom sign with impossible colour still passes, so a colour-consistency check against the sign class is a cheap cue. 100 ms persistence bounds the time window a temporal guard must cover.
notes: Short workshop paper; abstract and body read from the NDSS page and PDF text shown in a search result. Same group as Phantom of the ADAS (P2-P402).

venue: Proceedings Symposium on Vehicle Security & Privacy (VehicleSec 2024), poster

method: CARLA night scenes, Faster R-CNN Inception ResNet V2, flicker frequencies 0.5 to 60 Hz, weather variants; stopping-distance analysis.
data: CARLA simulation
reported_result: Poster text: 60 Hz flicker was the most effective frequency; adverse weather increased the effect.
relation_to_project: P-d and N4: the attacker modulates legitimate infrastructure lighting, so the flicker source is a real streetlight, the hardest benign look-alike. Simulation only; poster, not a full paper.
notes: Two-page poster read in full from the NDSS PDF text in a search result. Same first author as FLASH (P2-P2601). Simulation only.

category: O-F6 Detection, simulation, data and recovery for a light guard
title: Real-Time Adaptive Sensor Attack Detection in Autonomous Cyber-Physical Systems
venue: 2021 IEEE 27th Real-Time and Embedded Technology and Applications Symposium (RTAS)
key_idea: Detection delay and false-alarm rate trade off; a CUSUM detector on residuals between predicted and observed sensor values tunes its drift parameter online so alarms meet a safety deadline.
method: CNN-RNN behaviour predictor, CUSUM on residuals with adaptive drift, data-driven deadline estimator, lookup table from offline profiling.
data: AEGIS automotive CAN-bus data (about 2.5 h at 20 Hz) with injected modification, delay and replay attacks
reported_result: Paper text: detection delays between 0.3 s and 4.63 s for drift 0.2 to 0.8 across six attack types; false positives fall as drift rises; a fixed time-window detector alarmed after the deadline where the adaptive one did not.
relation_to_project: Method template for N5: a sequential residual detector with an explicit delay versus false-alarm trade-off and a deadline. Not camera data and not light attacks; the guard would apply the same CUSUM logic to illumination residuals.
notes: Accepted-manuscript text from the NSF public access repository seen in a search result. Same first author as the MetroCAD 2021 survey (P2-P2716).

title: Reproducible Evaluation of Camera Auto-Exposure Methods in the Field: Platform, Benchmark, and Lessons Learned
venue: IEEE Transactions on Field Robotics
key_idea: An exposure-bracketing emulator over the BorealHDR dataset lets auto-exposure methods be compared reproducibly; abrupt exposure-time changes are a main cause of visual SLAM failure, and sun glare defeated every method on one subset.
method: Backpack platform recording exposure brackets; emulator selects frames for any AE policy; ORB-SLAM2 evaluation; Mann-Whitney tests against a classical AE50 baseline.
data: BorealHDR dataset and its repeated-trajectory extension
reported_result: Preprint text: tested methods completed on average 27.5 trajectories, 47 percent of BorealHDR, without failure; the sun-glare subset Campus1 failed for all methods.
relation_to_project: Benign look-alike evidence for P-d and N4: auto-exposure jumps and sun glare alone break vision pipelines, so a guard must not treat exposure transients as attacks. Bracketed data can generate benign exposure sequences.

venue: Sensors
key_idea: A simulation chain from headlamp beam and spectrum to camera signal-to-noise ratio shows that the own vehicle's headlamp distribution strongly changes how much of the scene a night camera can recognise.
method: 16 measured production headlamp distributions, diffuse scene reflection, imaging-transfer and EMVA camera model, six-network recognition ensemble, WLTP speed weighting.
data: 16 measured headlamp light distributions; simulated scenes
reported_result: Abstract: WLTP-weighted coverage 18.95 to 53.48 percent across distributions (factor 2.82); correlation with a headlamp safety rating Pearson r = 0.68.
relation_to_project: Benign baseline for P-d at night: illumination differences between vehicles change detector evidence a lot without any attack, so night thresholds of a light guard need per-illumination calibration.

category: O-F6 Detection, simulation, data and recovery for a light guard
title: Adversarial Attack and Disturbance Detection by Hadamard-Coded Output Representations for Object Detection and Semantic Segmentation
venue: arXiv preprint
key_idea: Hadamard-coded outputs give object detectors redundant codewords; inconsistency between codeword bits signals both adversarial attacks and natural disturbances in a single forward pass.
method: Optimal decoding of Hadamard codewords by projection onto the probability simplex; inconsistency score used as detector; HadamardNet for detection and segmentation.
reported_result: Abstract: reports state-of-the-art perturbation detection for both tasks in a single pass with clean accuracy equal or close to reference (no numbers in the abstract).
relation_to_project: Closest output-side alternative to a guard (N1, N5): it flags attacks and disturbances alike, so it does not by itself separate light attacks from benign lighting; needs retraining the detector head.
notes: Preprint, not peer reviewed; published version not checked.

category: O-F6 Detection, simulation, data and recovery for a light guard
title: MirrorGuard: Defending LiDAR Perception against Passive Mirror Attacks
venue: arXiv preprint
key_idea: Physics-informed checks of the reflected path (aperture crossing, occlusion behind the mirror, double-reflection dimming) over several scans remove mirror-made phantom LiDAR returns before detection.
method: Three geometric and radiometric consistency cues accumulated over scans; removal of flagged returns; closed loop in CARLA with Autoware.
data: Real-world recordings of mirror attacks; CARLA closed loop
reported_result: Abstract: removes 96.31 percent of phantom returns at 98.30 percent precision, leaves 99.99 percent of other returns untouched, runs at 59 ms mean per scan on a CPU; no halt or crash in closed loop with the defense.
relation_to_project: LiDAR-only, kept because it is the clearest template for a reflection guard (design 3): physics cues, multi-frame evidence, benign-preservation and CPU latency all reported. A camera reflection guard should report the same four numbers.
notes: Preprint, not peer reviewed. LiDAR, not camera: kept by the brief's exception because the reflection lesson is explicit.

title: On the Vulnerability of Traffic Light Recognition Systems to Laser Illumination Attacks
venue: Proceedings Symposium on Vehicle Security & Privacy (VehicleSec 2024)
key_idea: Laser light aimed at a traffic light is scattered by its internal reflectors, so the camera sees a genuine-looking lit lamp; visible and invisible lasers flip recognised red or green state, even for switched-off lights.
method: Physical laser injection into incandescent traffic lights; three traffic light recognition models; controlled dynamic scenario.
data: Physical tests on incandescent traffic lights
reported_result: Abstract: works up to 25 m from the light; attack success 100 percent for misclassifying green and 86 percent for red in a controlled dynamic scenario.
relation_to_project: P-c and N3: the injected light sits inside the real lamp housing, so geometry and location checks pass; only colour, intensity history or lamp-state timing can expose it. Test case for a traffic-light branch of the guard.
notes: Abstract read from the DOI record in a search result (short paper). Same group as Invisible Reflections (P2-P309).

title: LED flicker: Root cause, impact and measurement for automotive imaging applications
venue: Electronic Imaging (IS&T, Autonomous Vehicles and Machines)
key_idea: PWM-driven LED lights above about 90 Hz look steady to people but appear on, off or banded to short-exposure cameras; the paper explains the sampling cause, ADAS impact and two flicker metrics.
method: Analysis of exposure versus PWM period; Flicker Detection Index and Percent Flicker measured on a camera with a controllable LED source.
data: Bench test with a PWM LED source
reported_result: Paper text: keeping a 90 Hz light from ever appearing off needs at least 11.111 ms exposure; in the example a 60 Hz light appeared off (index below 0.1) while a 150 Hz light stayed on (index 0.75, 1 percent residual flicker).
relation_to_project: Core benign look-alike for P-d and N4: legitimate LED signs, brake lights and traffic lights already flicker on camera, so a flicker cue alone cannot mean attack; the guard must model expected PWM behaviour.
notes: Full text shown in a search result from the IS&T library. Industry author; conference-journal format of Electronic Imaging.

category: O-F7 Benign look-alikes and false alarms
title: A review of IEEE P2020 flicker metrics
venue: Electronic Imaging (IS&T, Autonomous Vehicles and Machines)
key_idea: Reviews the IEEE P2020 automotive flicker metrics (modulation index, detection index, mitigation probability, beat frequency) and shows that the same average detectability can hide very different outage lengths.

data: Bench measurements at 121, 129 and 135 Hz
reported_result: Paper text: detection index 0.53, 0.4 and 0.5 at 121, 129 and 135 Hz, yet 121 Hz gave about 0.5 s outages while 135 Hz lost only single frames; P2020 recommends reporting the distribution of non-detections.
relation_to_project: Gives standard vocabulary and metrics for the benign flicker class (N4, N5): a guard's flicker features and its false-alarm tests can be stated in P2020 terms, and outage run-length matters more than averages.
notes: Text read from the IS&T library page shown in a search result. IEEE 2020 standard itself not read.

venue: Nature Communications
